questions.stem: How is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH, classified?
questions.explanation: The carbon bearing the OH group is bonded to three other carbon atoms, which makes it a tertiary alcohol. In a primary alcohol that carbon is bonded to one other carbon, and in a secondary alcohol to two.

questions.stem: Which of these is a secondary alcohol?
questions.explanation: In pentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, the carbon carrying the OH is bonded to two other carbons, so it is secondary. Pentan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are primary, and 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(OH)CH(CH₃)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain containing the OH has four carbons. Numbering from the end nearer the OH places it on carbon 2 and the methyl group on carbon 3. Numbering from the other end gives the higher locant 3 to the OH group.

questions.stem: Which pair of alcohols are position isomers of each other?
questions.explanation: Position isomers have the same carbon chain and functional group, with the group in a different position. Butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are chain isomers, while the other two pairs are members of a homologous series with different molecular formulas.

questions.stem: Ethanol (M = 46 g mol⁻¹) boils at 78 °C, but propane (M = 44 g mol⁻¹) boils at −42 °C. What best explains this?
options: Propane molecules have many more electrons, so their dispersion forces are weaker
Propane is an ionic compound, so its particles separate easily when heated
Ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other through their O-H groups
Ethanol molecules have stronger covalent bonds, which must break during boiling
questions.explanation: The O-H group lets ethanol form hydrogen bonds, which are much stronger than the dispersion forces that are the only attractions between propane molecules. The molecules have similar numbers of electrons, and no covalent bonds break on boiling.

questions.stem: Methanol, ethanol and propan-1-ol mix with water in all proportions, but solubility falls from butan-1-ol to octan-1-ol. Why?
options: Longer alcohols react with water to form insoluble products that separate out
The growing non-polar chain cannot hydrogen bond with water molecules
The O-H group becomes less polar as more carbon atoms are added to the chain
Longer alcohols form ionic bonds with each other, so they stay out of the water
questions.explanation: The OH group hydrogen bonds with water, but the hydrocarbon chain is non-polar and attracts water only weakly by dispersion forces. As the chain lengthens, the non-polar part dominates and the alcohol becomes less soluble.

questions.stem: The boiling points of ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol are 78, 97 and 118 °C. Which is the best estimate for the boiling point of pentan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: Each extra CH₂ group raises the boiling point by about 20 °C in this part of the series, because dispersion forces grow with chain length, so pentan-1-ol boils at about 138 °C. Doubling the value for butan-1-ol overstates the trend.

questions.stem: Butan-1-ol boils at 118 °C, but its isomer 2-methylpropan-2-ol boils at 82 °C. What best explains the difference?
options: The tertiary alcohol has no O-H bond, so it cannot form any hydrogen bonds
Butan-1-ol has more electrons per molecule, so its dispersion forces are stronger
The tertiary alcohol is ionic, so its particles are held less tightly
The compact tertiary molecule has weaker dispersion forces
questions.explanation: Both have the same formula and both can hydrogen bond. The near-spherical tertiary molecule has less surface contact with its neighbours, weakening dispersion forces, and the bulky groups around its OH make hydrogen bonding less effective, so it boils lower. The isomers have equal numbers of electrons.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of propan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: Each C₃H₈O gives 3CO₂ and 4H₂O, needing 10 O atoms, of which one comes from the alcohol, so 9/2 O₂ per molecule; doubling gives whole numbers. Forgetting the oxygen in the alcohol gives 5O₂, and CO as a product means incomplete combustion.

questions.stem: Compared with complete combustion, the incomplete combustion of an alcohol:
options: occurs in limited oxygen and produces carbon monoxide or soot
occurs in excess oxygen and produces only carbon dioxide and water
releases more energy per mole of alcohol and gives a blue flame
produces hydrogen gas and oxygen instead of carbon compounds
questions.explanation: When oxygen is limited, some carbon ends up as carbon monoxide or carbon (soot) instead of CO₂, less energy is released, and the flame is yellow and sooty. Water is still produced in both cases.

questions.stem: Enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹): methanol −726, ethanol −1367, propan-1-ol −2021, butan-1-ol −2676. What is the best estimate for pentan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: Each extra CH₂ makes the enthalpy of combustion about 650 kJ mol⁻¹ more negative, because burning the extra CH₂ forms one more CO₂ and one more H₂O, releasing a near-constant extra amount of energy. So pentan-1-ol is about −2676 − 654 = −3330 kJ mol⁻¹. Doubling butan-1-ol's value overstates it.

questions.stem: A spirit burner of propan-1-ol (M = 60.09 g mol⁻¹) loses 1.20 g while heating 250 g of water from 20.0 °C to 50.0 °C. Taking c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, what is the experimental enthalpy of combustion?
questions.explanation: q = mcΔT = 250 × 4.18 × 30.0 = 31 350 J = 31.35 kJ, and n = 1.20 / 60.09 = 0.0200 mol. ΔH = −31.35 / 0.0200 = −1.57 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹. The value 31.4 is q alone, and 26.1 is the energy per gram, not per mole.

questions.stem: A student's experimental enthalpy of combustion for an alcohol is much less negative than the accepted value. Which change would most improve the result?
options: Weighing the burner only at the start, as the final mass is not needed
Using a glass beaker instead of a copper can to hold the water
Shielding the burner and can from draughts, with a smaller gap
Using a larger mass of water so that the temperature rise is smaller
questions.explanation: The main error is heat lost to the surroundings rather than absorbed by the water. A draught shield, a short flame-to-can distance and a copper can, which conducts heat well, all help. A glass beaker conducts heat poorly, and both masses of the burner are needed to find the mass burnt.

questions.stem: Ethanol is heated with concentrated sulfuric acid. What are the products?
questions.explanation: Concentrated sulfuric (or phosphoric) acid removes water from the alcohol in a dehydration reaction, forming a C=C double bond: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O. Ethane would need hydrogen to be added, not water removed.

questions.stem: Butan-2-ol is dehydrated with concentrated phosphoric acid. Including geometric isomers, how many different alkenes can form?
questions.explanation: Water can be removed with an H from carbon 1, giving but-1-ene, or from carbon 3, giving but-2-ene, which exists as cis and trans isomers. That makes three alkenes. Forgetting the geometric isomers gives 2.

questions.stem: Propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate. What is the main organic product?
questions.explanation: Primary alcohols are oxidised first to an aldehyde and then, under reflux with excess oxidant, to the carboxylic acid. Refluxing returns the aldehyde to the flask, so it is oxidised further. Propanone would come from the secondary alcohol propan-2-ol.

questions.stem: Ethanol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. How can the aldehyde ethanal (boiling point 20 °C) be collected instead of ethanoic acid?
options: Use a tertiary alcohol instead, since it forms aldehydes more readily
Add sodium hydroxide so that the ethanoic acid changes back to ethanal
Distil off the ethanal as soon as it forms in the flask
Heat the mixture under reflux for a long time with excess dichromate
questions.explanation: Ethanal boils far below ethanol and ethanoic acid, so warming the mixture and distilling removes it from the oxidant as it forms. Refluxing would return it to the flask to be oxidised to the acid, and tertiary alcohols are not oxidised.

questions.stem: Butan-2-ol is oxidised with acidified potassium permanganate. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Oxidising a secondary alcohol gives a ketone, here butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃. Only primary alcohols give aldehydes and then carboxylic acids, and but-2-ene would come from dehydration, not oxidation.

questions.stem: Butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol are each shaken with concentrated hydrochloric acid containing zinc chloride. Which becomes cloudy fastest, as an insoluble chloroalkane forms?
questions.explanation: Substitution of the OH by Cl is fastest for tertiary alcohols, slower for secondary and very slow for primary alcohols at room temperature. The tertiary alcohol forms insoluble 2-chloro-2-methylpropane almost at once, turning the mixture cloudy.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the reaction of ethanol with hydrogen bromide?
questions.explanation: In this substitution reaction the bromine atom replaces the OH group, which leaves with the hydrogen of HBr as water. The products are bromoethane and water; the other equations are not balanced or describe impossible products.

questions.stem: 2-bromobutane is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide. What is the organic product?
questions.explanation: In this substitution reaction a hydroxide ion replaces the bromine on the same carbon atom: CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃ + OH⁻ → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ + Br⁻. The OH ends up where the Br was, on carbon 2.

questions.stem: 6.01 g of propan-1-ol (M = 60.09 g mol⁻¹) is oxidised, giving 5.19 g of propanoic acid (M = 74.08 g mol⁻¹). What is the percentage yield?
questions.explanation: The ratio is 1 : 1, so n(alcohol) = 6.01 / 60.09 = 0.100 mol and the theoretical mass of acid is 0.100 × 74.08 = 7.41 g. Yield = 5.19 / 7.41 × 100 = 70.0%. Comparing the masses directly, 5.19 / 6.01, gives 86.4%, and using the molar mass of propanal for the product gives 89.3%.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of making ethanol by the hydration of ethene over making it by fermentation?
options: It runs at room temperature and needs no catalyst at all
It absorbs carbon dioxide from the air as it produces ethanol
It is a fast, continuous process that gives nearly pure ethanol
It uses a renewable feedstock grown from crops each year
questions.explanation: Hydration of ethene with steam over an acid catalyst is fast, continuous and gives a high-purity product, but its ethene comes from crude oil, a non-renewable resource. Fermentation uses renewable plant sugars but is slow, works in batches and gives a dilute solution that must be distilled.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)COOH?
questions.explanation: The carboxyl carbon is carbon 1, so the chain has three carbons (propanoic acid) with a methyl group on carbon 2. A methyl on carbon 3 would simply make a longer chain, and butanoic acid is the unbranched isomer.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol both have M = 60 g mol⁻¹, but ethanoic acid boils at 118 °C and propan-1-ol at 97 °C. Why?
options: Propan-1-ol cannot form hydrogen bonds, as its O-H group is on a carbon chain
Ethanoic acid is an ionic compound, so it needs more energy to separate
The C=O and O-H groups of the acid allow more hydrogen bonding
Ethanoic acid has a longer carbon chain, so its dispersion forces are stronger
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group has both a C=O and an O-H, so acid molecules can hydrogen bond strongly in pairs (dimers) and to neighbours, giving stronger intermolecular forces than in the alcohol. Ethanoic acid has the shorter carbon chain, and both compounds hydrogen bond.

questions.stem: Pentane (M = 72), butan-1-ol (M = 74) and propanoic acid (M = 74) have similar molar masses. Which order runs from lowest to highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: Pentane has only dispersion forces (bp 36 °C). Butan-1-ol adds hydrogen bonding through its OH (118 °C). Propanoic acid has the strongest hydrogen bonding, through both C=O and O-H (141 °C).

questions.stem: Sodium carbonate solution is added to an unknown organic liquid, and bubbles of a gas that turns limewater milky are seen. Which functional group is present?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are acidic enough to react with carbonates, releasing carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky. Alcohols, alkenes and esters do not react with sodium carbonate in this way.

questions.stem: 3.00 g of ethanoic acid (M = 60.05 g mol⁻¹) reacts with excess sodium hydrogen carbonate: CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. What mass of CO₂ (M = 44.01 g mol⁻¹) forms?
questions.explanation: n(CH₃COOH) = 3.00 / 60.05 = 0.0500 mol, which gives 0.0500 mol of CO₂ by the 1 : 1 ratio. m = 0.0500 × 44.01 = 2.20 g. Assuming the mass is conserved between acid and gas gives 3.00 g.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The part from the acid, CH₃COO-, is ethanoate, and the alkyl group attached to the single-bonded oxygen has five carbons, pentyl. The alkyl group is named first: pentyl ethanoate. Reversing the parts gives ethyl pentanoate, a different ester.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: HCOO- comes from methanoic acid, so the ester is a methanoate, and the alkyl group on the oxygen is propyl. Methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃, is an isomer with the parts reversed.

questions.stem: Which ester forms when butan-1-ol reacts with methanoic acid?
questions.explanation: The alcohol supplies the alkyl group, butyl, and the acid supplies the -oate part, methanoate. Methyl butanoate would form from methanol and butanoic acid.

questions.stem: Counting carboxylic acids and esters only, how many functional group isomers have the molecular formula C₃H₆O₂?
questions.explanation: They are propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH), methyl ethanoate (CH₃COOCH₃) and ethyl methanoate (HCOOCH₂CH₃). Acids and esters with the same number of carbons share a general formula, so they are functional group isomers.

questions.stem: Methyl ethanoate boils at 57 °C, while its isomer propanoic acid boils at 141 °C. Why?
options: The ester has fewer electrons, so its dispersion forces are much weaker
The ester breaks down on heating, so it boils at a lower temperature
Ester molecules have no O-H group, so they cannot hydrogen bond to each other
Ester molecules are non-polar, so only dispersion forces act between them
questions.explanation: Esters are polar, with dipole-dipole forces, but they lack an O-H group, so their molecules cannot hydrogen bond to one another. The isomeric acid hydrogen bonds strongly. As isomers, both have the same number of electrons.

questions.stem: Esters such as ethyl ethanoate catch fire more easily than carboxylic acids of similar molar mass. Which property explains this?
options: Esters are more volatile, so flammable vapour forms more readily
Esters contain more oxygen atoms, so they need no air at all to burn
Esters are ionic, so they react with oxygen faster than molecular acids
Esters have stronger intermolecular forces, so their vapour is denser
questions.explanation: Without hydrogen bonding between molecules, esters have weaker intermolecular forces and lower boiling points, so they evaporate readily and form flammable vapour at lower temperatures. Combustibility in the laboratory depends largely on volatility.

questions.stem: When an ester is prepared in the laboratory, why is the mixture heated under reflux?
options: The ester distils off as it forms, giving a pure product at once
The reflux condenser removes water, so no catalyst is needed
The mixture is kept cold so that the ester does not decompose
Volatile reactants and products condense and return to the flask
questions.explanation: Esterification is slow, so the mixture is heated for some time. The vertical condenser cools the vapours of the volatile alcohol, acid and ester so they run back into the flask instead of escaping. A catalyst is still needed.

questions.stem: In an esterification, why is concentrated sulfuric acid added to the alcohol and carboxylic acid?
options: It catalyses the reaction and absorbs water, favouring the ester
It is a reactant that provides the oxygen atoms for the ester
It neutralises the carboxylic acid so that the ester can form
It dissolves the ester so that it can be separated from water
questions.explanation: Concentrated sulfuric acid speeds up the reaction as a catalyst. Esterification is an equilibrium, and because the acid also absorbs the water produced, the equilibrium shifts towards the ester, raising the yield.

questions.stem: After refluxing, the crude ester is shaken with sodium carbonate solution in a separating funnel, then distilled. What is the purpose of the sodium carbonate wash?
options: To react with leftover carboxylic acid and sulfuric acid, removing them
To react with the ester, converting it to a salt that is easier to purify
To act as a catalyst for the remaining alcohol and acid to react
To dry the ester by absorbing the water dissolved in it completely
questions.explanation: The carbonate reacts with the acids to form water-soluble salts and carbon dioxide, which stay in the aqueous layer. The ester is insoluble and forms a separate layer, which is then distilled to separate it from any remaining alcohol.

questions.stem: Which pair of monomers can form a polyester by condensation polymerisation?
questions.explanation: To build a chain, each monomer needs two functional groups, so that ester links can form at both ends, with water released each time. Ethanol and ethanoic acid have one group each and form only a single ester molecule. Ethene and chloroethene form addition polymers.

questions.stem: 4.60 g of ethanol (M = 46.07 g mol⁻¹) reacts with excess ethanoic acid, producing 6.60 g of ethyl ethanoate (M = 88.11 g mol⁻¹). What is the percentage yield?
questions.explanation: n(ethanol) = 4.60 / 46.07 = 0.0998 mol, so the theoretical mass of ester is 0.0998 × 88.11 = 8.80 g. Yield = 6.60 / 8.80 × 100 = 75.0%. A yield above 100% would come from dividing the actual mass by the mass of ethanol.

questions.stem: Which reaction pathway makes ethyl ethanoate using ethene as the only organic starting material?
options: Add hydrogen to ethene to give ethane, then react the ethane with ethanoic acid under reflux
Dehydrate ethene to ethanol, reduce the ethanol to ethanoic acid, then esterify with ethene
Hydrate ethene to ethanol, oxidise some ethanol to ethanoic acid, then esterify with the rest
Oxidise ethene to ethanoic acid, then react the acid with more ethene and an acid catalyst
questions.explanation: Ethene and steam give ethanol over an acid catalyst. Part of the ethanol is oxidised with acidified dichromate to ethanoic acid, which is then refluxed with the remaining ethanol and concentrated sulfuric acid to form the ester. Esters form from an alcohol and an acid, not from an alkene or alkane.
